html:
The Battle of Sedan was fought on 1 September 1870 at Sedan in northeast France, near the Belgian border. German armies led by Prussia surrounded a French army and captured the emperor Napoleon III with about 100,000 men.

It decided the Franco-Prussian War. Bismarck wanted a war that would bring the south German states into a united Germany, and France declared war in July 1870. By August one French army was shut up in Metz. A second, under Marshal MacMahon and with the emperor, marched to free it and was pushed back to Sedan, a small fortress in the valley of the Meuse. The Prussian general Helmuth von Moltke closed a ring around it and put hundreds of guns on the hills. French cavalry charged again and again and could not break out. Napoleon surrendered the next day.

Two days later a republic was declared in Paris. The Germans besieged the city, and in January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles; see Germany. France lost Alsace and part of Lorraine. Sedan made Germany the strongest power in Europe and left France wanting revenge, which shaped the road to 1914.
